rules.label: VO2max floor, missions with microgravity EVAs
notes: 'as determined by either direct or indirect measures' (requirement text).

action.label: EVA assignment not cleared
action.text: EVA assignment not cleared: this VO2max test is below the floor NASA-STD-3001 sets for missions with microgravity EVAs. Review the exercise prescription with the Crew Medical Officer and retest before an EVA is assigned.

source.rationale: [V1 4001] says crewmembers 'shall maintain' this capacity, so a test below the floor is an exercise-prescription and EVA-assignment matter: it needs attention, not immediate action (Table 10.3-1 Caution), and it says nothing about the heart or the lungs. The assignment decision belongs to the Crew Medical Officer, the flight surgeon and Mission Control, not to LANDFALL.

rules.label: Cabin ppCO2, one-hour average

source.rationale: 80% of the limit (2.4 of 3 mmHg). LANDFALL uses the same 80% convention for every ceiling; NASA-STD-3001 publishes no 'approaching' level.

notes: Three CO2 windows are easy to confuse: this NASA standard is a 1-hour average. The ISS flight rule (24-hour average) and research findings (7-day average) are different numbers and are not used here.
Category PEL is assigned by shape (a ceiling on exposure over a time window). NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 does not itself label [V2 6004] a PEL.
The defensible health claim is headache risk; LANDFALL makes no claim that CO2 causes a cognitive deficit.
The value comes from the vehicle (ECLSS); the vehicle caution and warning system owns any alarm.

action.label: Cabin CO2 at or near the 1-hour limit

source.rationale: The defensible health claim for CO2 is headache risk (rule note); the vehicle's caution and warning system owns the alarm, so LANDFALL only points to the procedure and the Crew Medical Officer.

notes: Compliant (within) while the >=10 MeV integral proton flux is below this level; 'outside' means S5 or higher has been reached. pfu = particles cm^-2 s^-1 sr^-1.
NOAA operational scale, not a NASA crew-health limit and no NASA requirement ID.
Outside (S3 or higher) is a Warning: the rule carries the shelter action, which is immediate (Table 10.3-1).

rules.label: Mars-orbit space-weather monitor: >=10 MeV protons at the NOAA S3 level

source.rationale: [V2 6164] requires the radiation monitoring system to alert the crew 'when radiation exposure rates exceed predefined thresholds' and leaves the threshold to the program. At Mars no NOAA alert reaches the crew. The scenario assumes an external space-weather monitor above the atmosphere, in Mars orbit, whose >=10 MeV proton reading is relayed to the habitat locally, with no Earth link: the in-situ extravehicular monitoring of 'proton flux spectra' that [V2 6165] requires. LANDFALL reuses NOAA's S3 threshold (10^3 pfu at >=10 MeV, rule ops_noaa_s3) on that reading; NOAA does not define its scale away from Earth, so applying it at Mars is ours. The vehicle's radiation monitoring system raises the alarm ([V2 6164]); this rule opens the health case that follows.

notes: Same variable as the NOAA rules; applies_to keeps exactly one of the two rule sets active.

Scenario assumption: the demo values are the GOES-7 October 1989 >=10 MeV replay, with no radial-distance or atmospheric correction. A monitor on the surface would read less, because the atmosphere stops the lower-energy protons; that is why the scenario's monitor sits above it, in orbit.
Outside (S3 or higher) is a Warning: the rule carries the shelter action, which is immediate (Table 10.3-1).

rules.label: 24-h urine output (renal stone case)

source.doc: NASA HRP Evidence Report: Risk of Renal Stone Formation (Stratton, Lumpkins & Antonsen, approved September 23, 2024; NTRS 20240012429)
source.citation: Stratton E, Lumpkins S, Antonsen E. Evidence Report: Risk of Renal Stone Formation. NASA Human Research Program, Exploration Medical Capabilities Element, Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center, Houston, TX. Approved for public release September 23, 2024. NTRS 20240012429.
source.verbatim: the risk for renal stone development increases when urinary volume drops below 1.5 liters/day; therefore, an effective hydration countermeasure should be sufficient to produce 2.5-3 liters/day of urine volume (Kassemi and Thompson 2016b)
source.note: NASA-authored HRP evidence report, not a standard: it carries no requirement ID. The scanned 2024 PDF was read by OCR; the identical sentence is machine-readable in the 2017 edition (Sibonga JD, Pietrzyk R. Evidence Report: Risk of Renal Stone Formation. NASA HRP, approved for public release May 15, 2017. NTRS 20170004709, p. 14). The underlying source is the Kassemi and Thompson 2016 model cited there.

approach_at.rationale: Below 2,500 mL/day the hydration countermeasure is short of its 2.5-3 L/day target (same sentence).

notes: Not a NASA standard and not a NASA alert threshold: the numbers come from a NASA HRP evidence report. Outside = below 1,500 mL/day (where the report says stone risk rises); approaching = below 2,500 mL/day (short of the 2.5-3 L/day countermeasure target).
An informal urine-output target that circulates without a NASA source is not used; the numbers here come only from the evidence-report sentence quoted in the source.
Context: [V2 6109] Table 6.3-1 requires the vehicle to provide a minimum of 2.5 L of potable water for hydration per crewmember per day.
Capped at caution: a low-urine day is something to act on, not a warning.
